title: PyRUA-Dex: Learning Programmatic Policies for Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation with Coding Agents
author: Feixiang Ruan, Guodong Lv, Kewei Zhang
snippet: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a…
excerpt: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.

title: DyLoMo-DiT: Dynamic Looped Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Transformers
author: Lernie Li, Yuanliu Liu, Pengfei Xiong
snippet: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) scale model capacity by increasing both parameter count and computation. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants expand parameter capacity while keeping per-token computation roughly fixed, but still require substantial parameter storage. In this paper…
excerpt: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) scale model capacity by increasing both parameter count and computation. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants expand parameter capacity while keeping per-token computation roughly fixed, but still require substantial parameter storage. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Looped MoE DiT (DyLoMo-DiT), which reuses parameters rather than adding them: a weight-shared loop repeatedly applies the middle layers, while sparse experts allocate parameter capacity across tokens. This design deepens the network without adding parameters, freeing the parameter budget for other uses, such as more experts or more distinct layers. It also allocates compute dynamically, varying the number of passes across noise levels. Experiments show that DyLoMo-DiT makes more effective use of parameter and compute budgets, with further gains from assigning more passes to low-noise steps. On ImageNet 256times256, DyLoMo-DiT reduces FID by 11-24% relative to DiT and 36-56% relative to DiT-MoE at matched parameter and compute budgets. For text-to-image generation, a scaled DyLoMo-DiT achieves a higher GenEval score than FLUX.1 (0.714 vs. 0.673), with less than one tenth of its active parameters (1.05B vs. 12B).

title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification
author: Xingjian Ran, Xiaoye Mo, Sihao Liu
snippet: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to…
excerpt: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.

The sparse layers select their context with a pooled indexer: the keys of 4 consecutive tokens are pooled by a per-channel softmax of a gate plus a position bias, normed, and rotated at the position of the first token. title: SEEK: Self-Evolution through Execution Knowledge for Agentic Robot Manipulation
author: Zeyang Guan, Qihao Zhao, Rui Gong
snippet: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the model's working context. Once the task ends…
excerpt: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the model's working context. Once the task ends, it loses this execution knowledge, such as how to carry a bowl between two grippers. On the next attempt at the task, the robot may take just as long and repeat the same mistakes. To avoid this repetition, robots must retain execution knowledge across attempts. Yet replaying past actions is insufficient, because their effects depend on the current conditions. Procedures that determine actions from the current scene address this, but when they meet conditions that earlier attempts did not cover, revising them requires the measured effects of earlier actions. We therefore propose SEEK, an agentic framework that retains both, enabling robots to improve across attempts while keeping the underlying model fixed. To adapt retained knowledge to the current scene, SEEK adopts a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) that encodes manipulation as executable procedures and determines each action from current observations. As the robot executes these procedures, SEEK records the measured effects of its actions, including those from failed attempts, in a Persistent Action-Effect Bank (PAEB). Where a retained procedure applies, it acts without a model request; where it meets a condition it does not cover, this evidence guides its revision. On RoboDojo, knowledge retained over ten attempts raises SEEK's average task score from 27.0 to 54.4 and its success rate from 19.7% to 48.0% across all 42 tasks. On 34 of these tasks with GPT-6.2 Astra, SEEK reaches 80.1 after five attempts, against 49.6 for the same model acting directly, and uses 77.6% fewer model requests.

GATED_DELTA_NET_CACHE_FUSION copies the final state into the cache and then reads the copy, so the cache kept its old contents. Write such a node back through its view_src, as is already done when nothing reads it. Model graphs are unchanged. ggml-openvino: keep the rest of the buffer in a partial in-place FILL An in-place FILL on a view into part of a larger buffer produced only the filled values. Its output stands for the whole in-place source, so the write-back put those values at the start of the buffer and not at the view's offset. For a contiguous view with a static shape, build the whole buffer: the elements before the view, the filled values, then the elements after it. Add NodeContext::get_inplace_op_src() to detect the in-place case. ggml-openvino: fix softplus precision for large negative inputs softplus was computed as relu(x) + log(1 + exp(-|x|)). The SOFTPLUS test case with inputs in [-16.6, -16] fails on CPU and GPU. title: Tell HN: Finality is like the speed of light to LLMs from the labs
author: figassis
snippet: I think you've all noticed the "one more thing" with AI, and the many articles to fix it, and that they don't really fix anything at all. If your task ends, so does token spend, so if you ask an LLM to draw a square (metaphor for a moderately complex system), it will forever…
excerpt: I think you've all noticed the "one more thing" with AI, and the many articles to fix it, and that they don't really fix anything at all. If your task ends, so does token spend, so if you ask an LLM to draw a square (metaphor for a moderately complex system), it will forever draw you an approximation of a square, and after stopping it will always tell you that there is still more work to do. Not matter how much you try to force it to finish it just does not. As if physically it can approach but never reach finality. What has been your experience? Has it improved? How?
